newsitem.title: USA: Stocks up on bargain hunting; bonds edge down.
newsitem.headline: Stocks up on bargain hunting; bonds edge down.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks posted their strongest rally in three weeks on Monday as investors sought bargains after last week's sell-off.
Bonds edged lower, while the dollar rose amid expectations that interest rates will remain low in Japan and Europe and move higher in the United States.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 60.21 points at 6,451.90, its largest gain since a 101-point surge on March 24. Last week, the market was in a bearish mood as it fell nearly 135 points on interest rate worries.
In the broader market, declining issues still led advances 1,425 to 1,037 on moderate volume of 406 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts said nervous investors found some relief when a series of leading multinational companies, including Coca-Cola Co. and General Motors Corp., announced first-quarter profits that exceeded Wall Street's estimates.
"Today's rally suggests select stocks with good earnings may put some bounce back in the market," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
Analysts cautioned, however, that market sentiment remained guarded, particularly with key inflation data due in Tuesday's Consumer Price Index.

"In general, results are coming in better than expected, but we've still got a test tomorrow in the CPI," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates. "Today certainly doesn't mean we're out of the woods."
Stocks were rattled Friday by news that wholesale prices in March chalked up an unexpected 0.4 percent rise in the so-called core rate, which excludes often-volatile food and energy costs.

The looming report on inflation at the retail level held the bond market in check. The Treasury's 30-year bond lost 1/32, or 31 cents per $1,000 face value, leaving its yield unchanged at Friday's close of 7.17 percent.
The quiet bond market left stock traders free to focus on generally favourable earnings news.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 1.7310 German marks, up from 1.7205 marks late Friday. The dollar climbed to 126.63 Japanese yen from 126.12 yen.
Wheat prices soared after freezing weather hit the developing winter wheat crop in the United States, threatening to cut both production and exports this year.
Wheat for May delivery at the Chicago Board of Trade jumped the 20-cent-per-bushel daily trading limit at the opening bell and stayed there. May wheat closed at $4.23, up 20 cents a bushel.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices ended higher on a report linking Iran, the third largest oil exporter, to the 1996 bombing of a U.S. military compound in Saudi Arabia. The report came at time when diplomatic tensions are already high between the West and Iran.
Crude oil for delivery in May ended 37 cents a barrel higher at $19.90. May unleaded gasoline closed up 1.08 cents at 61.96 cents a gallon, and May heating oil up 0.80 cent at 54.67 cents gallon.
Overseas, London's benchmark FTSE 100 index of leading shares shed 19.0 points to settle at 4,251.7. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average shed 154.51 points to close at 17,692.47.
